bibl.title: The importance of mixed selectivity in complex cognitive tasks

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mixed selectivity in prefrontal cortex neurons and the dimensionality of the population representation it produces
span.quote: Single-neuron activity in prefrontal cortex (PFC) is tuned to mixtures of multiple task-related aspects. Such mixed selectivity is highly heterogeneous, seemingly disordered and therefore difficult to interpret.

span.label: what functional role the heterogeneous, hard-to-interpret mixed selectivity of PFC neurons plays
span.quote: The predominance of these mixed selectivity neurons appears to be a hallmark of PFC and other brain structures involved in cognition. Understanding such neural representations has been a major conceptual challenge in the field.

span.label: reinterprets seemingly disordered tuning as the signature of a high-dimensional code, measures that dimensionality through classifier capacity, and shows it collapses when the animal errs
span.quote: Specifically we found that: 1) the populations of recorded neurons encode distributed information that is not contained in classical selectivity to individual task aspects, 2) the recorded neural representations are high-dimensional, and 3) the dimensionality of the recorded neural representations predicts behavioural performance.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: This advantage originates from the highly diverse non-linear selectivity to mixtures of task-relevant variables, a signature of high-dimensional neural representations.

span.label: mixed selectivity in prefrontal cortex
span.quote: Single-neuron activity in prefrontal cortex (PFC) is tuned to mixtures of multiple task-related aspects.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: We analysed the activity of 237 lateral PFC neurons (area 46) recorded in two monkeys during the trial epochs that precede and include the two-object delay period.

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: In the error trials this component of the selectivity is disrupted, leading to a collapse in dimensionality, which impairs the ability of downstream readout neurons to produce the correct response.

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: The change in dimensionality may be caused by the excessive variability of sources that are not task-relevant.

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: This advantage originates from the highly diverse non-linear selectivity to mixtures of task-relevant variables, a signature of high-dimensional neural representations.

span.label: mechanisms
span.quote: A theoretical argument ( Supplementary Section S.18 ) shows that neurons with a strong non-linear mixed selectivity are more sensitive than pure selectivity neurons to the task irrelevant sources of variability.

span.label: dimensionality is estimated by counting how many binary classifications a linear classifier can implement, since that number grows exponentially with dimension
span.quote: Our method relies on the observation that the number of binary classifications that can be implemented by a linear classifier grows exponentially with the number of dimensions of the neural representations of the patterns of activities to be classified ( Supplementary Methods M.1 ). Hence dimensionality can be estimated by counting the number of binary classifications that can be implemented by a linear classifier.

span.label: the estimate is converted by d = log2(Nc), valid when the number of inputs is large enough
span.quote: The total number of implementable binary classifications N c is related to the estimated dimensionality d of the representations through the expression d = log 2 N c , when the number of inputs is sufficiently large

span.label: only non-linear mixed selectivity can raise dimensionality: pure selectivity and linear mixing generate low-dimensional representations
span.quote: This is because a set of neurons whose responses are selective only to individual task-relevant aspects, or even to linear sums of multiple aspects (linear mixed selectivity) can only generate low-dimensional representations. Higher dimensional representations can be produced by including neurons whose responses cannot be explained as a linear sum of aspect-related responses, i.e. neurons with non-linear mixed selectivity

span.label: classical selectivity is removed by adding noise that equalises average responses while preserving differences between individual conditions
span.quote: Classical selectivity to a given task-relevant aspect is removed from every recorded neuron, by adding noise that equalizes average responses preserving the differences between the individual conditions

span.label: averaging over conditions to test classical selectivity is itself what discards the distributed information
span.quote: The operation of averaging over all conditions corresponding to a particular task type (for each task type there are 12 possible combinations of the sample visual objects) may, however, result in discarding important information.

span.label: the proposed cause of the error-trial collapse: non-linear mixing is more sensitive than pure selectivity to task-irrelevant variability, so it is the most useful and the most fragile component
span.quote: A theoretical argument ( Supplementary Section S.18 ) shows that neurons with a strong non-linear mixed selectivity are more sensitive than pure selectivity neurons to the task irrelevant sources of variability. Non-linear mixed selectivity is most useful but also most fragile.

span.label: non-simultaneously recorded neurons are combined into pseudo-simultaneous population vectors, discarding temporal correlations
span.quote: Neurons that were not recorded simultaneously were combined as pseudo-simultaneous population activity patterns as explained in Supplementary Methods M.5 . The temporal correlations that were neglected with this procedure do not seem to appreciably affect the decoding accuracy

span.label: Errors could only be analysed in the recall task because the recognition task yielded too few of them.
span.quote: We tested this prediction by analysing the errors made by the monkeys in the recall task (there were too few errors in the recognition task).

span.label: Non-simultaneously recorded neurons were combined into pseudo-simultaneous population patterns, neglecting temporal correlations.
span.quote: Neurons that were not recorded simultaneously were combined as pseudo-simultaneous population activity patterns as explained in Supplementary Methods M.5 .

span.label: The argument is framed for linear readouts; whether it holds for more complex non-linear readouts is left open.
span.quote: It is legitimate to ask whether these considerations would still be valid if we consider more complex non-linear readouts.

span.label: Dimensionality expansion by single-neuron dendritic non-linearities is not ruled out.
span.quote: Our results do not exclude the functional importance of such dendritic processes.

span.label: the measured dimensionality is bounded above by the number of experimental conditions, and the recorded data reach that maximum
span.quote: Accordingly, the dimensionality is bounded by the total number of distinct conditions c .

span.label: dimensionality is notoriously difficult to estimate in the presence of noise, which is why an indirect method was needed
span.quote: As this is notoriously difficult in the presence of noise (see Supplementary Sections S.10 and [ 15 ]), we adopted a novel strategy that exploits the relation between dimensionality and the performance of a linear classifier reading out the neural activity

span.label: non-linear transformations implemented in dendrites could expand dimensionality invisibly, leaving firing-rate representations low-dimensional
span.quote: It is legitimate to ask whether these considerations would still be valid if we consider more complex non-linear readouts. For example, some of the transformations which increase the dimensionality of the neural representations could be implemented at the level of individual neurons by exploiting dendritic non-linearities. Our results do not exclude the functional importance of such dendritic processes. They do, however, tend to argue against a scenario where all important non-linear transformations are carried out at the level of single neurons, a situation where dimensionality expansion could happen in a “hidden way”, and the observable representations provided by the neuronal firing rates could therefore be low-dimensional.

span.label: high dimensionality is not strictly necessary for rich dynamics or complex tasks; the claim is that it simplifies circuit design
span.quote: Although high dimensionality is not strictly necessary for generating rich dynamics and performing complex tasks, it is known to greatly simplify the design of local neural circuits

span.label: the causal account of the collapse is offered explicitly as speculation
span.quote: It is tempting to speculate about the causes of this dimensionality collapse. Nonlinear mixed selectivity can change in a way that is compatible with our observations when neurons integrate multiple sources of information, which include those that are relevant for the task and those that are not under experimental control.

span.label: temporal correlations are discarded by the pseudo-simultaneous construction
span.quote: Neurons that were not recorded simultaneously were combined as pseudo-simultaneous population activity patterns as explained in Supplementary Methods M.5 . The temporal correlations that were neglected with this procedure do not seem to appreciably affect the decoding accuracy

span.label: the error analysis rests on 121 neurons with enough error trials, and only in the recall task
span.quote: These analyses were carried out on a subset dataset of 121 neurons that were recorded in as many correct as error trials during the recall task.

span.label: the analysis of the recorded population was designed from machine-learning theory about how learning principles operate in neuronal circuits
span.quote: Motivated by recent theoretical advances in understanding how machine learning principles play out in the functioning of neuronal circuits

span.label: the coding strategy of support vector machines is used as the interpretive frame for what mixed selectivity is doing
span.quote: This analysis revealed that the observed mixed selectivity can be naturally understood as a signature of the information encoding strategy of state-of-the-art classifiers like support vector machines

span.label: the perceptron learning rule is imported as the supervised procedure by which a readout neuron's weights would be adjusted
span.quote: just as it allows them to implement arbitrary binary classifications by modifying the weights of a readout neuron (using, for instance, a supervised procedure like the perceptron learning rule

span.label: the kernel-machine insight that projecting into a high-dimensional space lets a linear classifier implement more functions, imported as the interpretation of PFC tuning
span.quote: Moreover, mixed selectivity offers a significant computational advantage over specialized responses in terms of the repertoire of input-output functions implementable by readout neurons. This advantage originates from the highly diverse non-linear selectivity to mixtures of task-relevant variables, a signature of high-dimensional neural representations.

span.label: counting implementable dichotomies as a measure of representational capacity, used here as the dimensionality estimator
span.quote: Our method relies on the observation that the number of binary classifications that can be implemented by a linear classifier grows exponentially with the number of dimensions of the neural representations of the patterns of activities to be classified ( Supplementary Methods M.1 ). Hence dimensionality can be estimated by counting the number of binary classifications that can be implemented by a linear classifier.

span.label: the observation that firing rates are less variable on faster-reaction-time trials, used as the analogy for variability driving the error-trial collapse
span.quote: A theoretical argument ( Supplementary Section S.18 ) shows that neurons with a strong non-linear mixed selectivity are more sensitive than pure selectivity neurons to the task irrelevant sources of variability. Non-linear mixed selectivity is most useful but also most fragile.

span.label: dimensionality here is a property of CONDITION space: the minimal number of coordinate axes needed to place one firing-rate vector per experimental condition. It is not a statement about time courses across cells
span.quote: The dimensionality of a neural representation in a given time bin is a property of a set of vectors, each of which represents the firing rates of N recorded neurons in one experimental condition. The pattern of activity encoded in each such vector can be thought of as a point in an N -dimensional space. Over a set of such points, the dimensionality we refer to is defined as the minimal number of coordinate axes that are needed to specify the position of all points

span.label: high-dimensional is therefore a bounded claim in this paper - the ceiling is the number of conditions, here 24, and the data reach it
span.quote: Accordingly, the dimensionality is bounded by the total number of distinct conditions c .

span.label: mixed selectivity means tuning to a mixture of task aspects; only the NON-LINEAR kind raises dimensionality, and the paper keeps linear and non-linear mixing strictly apart
span.quote: This is because a set of neurons whose responses are selective only to individual task-relevant aspects, or even to linear sums of multiple aspects (linear mixed selectivity) can only generate low-dimensional representations. Higher dimensional representations can be produced by including neurons whose responses cannot be explained as a linear sum of aspect-related responses, i.e. neurons with non-linear mixed selectivity

span.label: classically selective is defined by a significant difference in averages across a task aspect - and the paper's point is that this test discards the information it is looking for
span.quote: A neuron is conventionally said to be selective to a task-relevant aspect if it responds differentially to the values of the parameters characterizing that aspect. A neuron is, for instance, selective to task type, if its average responses in recall and recognition task trials are significantly different.

span.label: pure selectivity means responding to one aspect at a time; it is the foil, simulated rather than recorded
span.quote: However, it is important to note that high-dimensional representations could also originate from more “orderly” responses, in which each neuron behaves as a “grandmother cell” that responds only to a single experimental condition – in our case to one out of 24.

span.label: builds-on → the monkey object sequence memory dataset of ref [3]
span.quote: To characterize the statistics and understand the functional role of mixed selectivity, we analysed neural activity recorded in the prefrontal cortex of monkeys during a sequence memory task [ 3 ].

span.label: builds-on → machine-learning-inspired circuit theory, refs [4]-[10]
span.quote: Motivated by recent theoretical advances in understanding how machine learning principles play out in the functioning of neuronal circuits [ 4 ], [ 5 ], [ 6 ], [ 7 ], [ 8 ], [ 9 ], [ 10 ], we devised a new analysis of the recorded population activity.

span.label: extends → prior linear-readout decoding studies, refs [17], [18]
span.quote: Previous studies have already shown that a linear readout is often sufficient to decode particular task aspects or to perform specific tasks (see e.g. [ 17 ], [ 18 ]).

span.label: reinterprets → the heterogeneous, seemingly disordered tuning that reverse-engineering approaches treat as noise
span.quote: Neurophysiology experiments in behaving animals are often analysed and modelled with a reverse engineering perspective, with the more or less explicit intention to identify highly specialized components with distinct functional roles in the behaviour under study. Physiologists often find the components they are looking for, contributing to the understanding of the functions and the underlying mechanisms of various brain areas, but they are also bewildered by numerous observations that are difficult to interpret.

span.label: extends → previous demonstrations that a linear readout suffices to decode particular task aspects
span.quote: Here, by showing that the neural representations are high-dimensional, we demonstrate that ANY binary choice task involving the 24 experimental conditions that we analysed could be performed by a linear readout.

span.label: supports → model circuits that expand dimensionality by random non-linear mixing
span.quote: In recent models [ 5 ], [ 6 ], [ 7 ], [ 8 ], [ 9 ], [ 10 ], the dimensionality of the neuronal representations is expanded by mixing in a non-linear way the different sources of information in a population of randomly connected neurons. The resulting neuronal representations are high-dimensional (see e.g. [ 20 ]), like those observed in PFC, and consistent with high dimensionality, the neurons exhibit mixed selectivity which is diverse across time (i.e. in different epochs of the trials) and space (i.e. across different neurons). Random connectivity in small brain regions has been suggested based on anatomical reconstructions [ 21 ] and recently observed in the connections from the olfactory bulb to the olfactory cortex

span.label: qualifies → its own claim, by allowing that dendritic non-linearities could hide the expansion
span.quote: It is legitimate to ask whether these considerations would still be valid if we consider more complex non-linear readouts. For example, some of the transformations which increase the dimensionality of the neural representations could be implemented at the level of individual neurons by exploiting dendritic non-linearities. Our results do not exclude the functional importance of such dendritic processes. They do, however, tend to argue against a scenario where all important non-linear transformations are carried out at the level of single neurons, a situation where dimensionality expansion could happen in a “hidden way”, and the observable representations provided by the neuronal firing rates could therefore be low-dimensional.

span.label: contradicts → the grandmother-cell account of how high dimensionality could arise
span.quote: We ruled out this scenario in our data by verifying that PFC representations are rather dense ( Supplementary Section S.11 ) and that the sparsest responses are not a major contributor to the observed high dimensionality

span.label: non-linear mixed selectivity —causes→ dimensionality
span.quote: This is because a set of neurons whose responses are selective only to individual task-relevant aspects, or even to linear sums of multiple aspects (linear mixed selectivity) can only generate low-dimensional representations. Higher dimensional representations can be produced by including neurons whose responses cannot be explained as a linear sum of aspect-related responses, i.e. neurons with non-linear mixed selectivity

span.label: linear mixed selectivity —contrasted-with→ non-linear mixed selectivity
span.quote: This is because a set of neurons whose responses are selective only to individual task-relevant aspects, or even to linear sums of multiple aspects (linear mixed selectivity) can only generate low-dimensional representations. Higher dimensional representations can be produced by including neurons whose responses cannot be explained as a linear sum of aspect-related responses, i.e. neurons with non-linear mixed selectivity

span.label: dimensionality —operationalised-as→ binary classifications
span.quote: Our method relies on the observation that the number of binary classifications that can be implemented by a linear classifier grows exponentially with the number of dimensions of the neural representations of the patterns of activities to be classified ( Supplementary Methods M.1 ). Hence dimensionality can be estimated by counting the number of binary classifications that can be implemented by a linear classifier.

span.label: classical selectivity —contrasted-with→ mixed selectivity
span.quote: The operation of averaging over all conditions corresponding to a particular task type (for each task type there are 12 possible combinations of the sample visual objects) may, however, result in discarding important information.

span.label: pure selectivity —distinct-from→ grandmother cell
span.quote: However, it is important to note that high-dimensional representations could also originate from more “orderly” responses, in which each neuron behaves as a “grandmother cell” that responds only to a single experimental condition – in our case to one out of 24.

Hence dimensionality can be estimated by counting the number of binary classifications that can be implemented by a linear classifier.

span.label: Task type and both cue identities can still be decoded from the PFC population after each neuron's classical selectivity to that aspect has been removed, so the information is distributed across the population rather than carried by individually selective cells.
span.quote: Crucially, all task-relevant aspects can be decoded even when classical selectivity is removed.

span.label: During the two-object delay the recorded PFC population supports the maximum possible number of binary classifications, i.e. it attains the maximal dimensionality of 24 set by the 24 experimental conditions.
span.quote: For the recorded data (black line) N c reaches 2 24 , the value that corresponds to the maximal dimensionality d = 24, given by all possible combinations of cue 1 object, cue 2 object and task type are 24 (dashed line).

span.label: A simulated population of pure selectivity neurons with the same noise level spans fewer than 8 dimensions in the same epoch, far below the recorded population.
span.quote: On the other hand, representations based on pure selectivity (grey line) generate less than 8 dimensions.

span.label: The dimensionality of the PFC representation drops on trials where the monkey makes an error, so dimensionality tracks behavioural success.
span.quote: As predicted, the dimensionality decreases in the error trials.

span.label: On error trials the identities of the two cues are still decoded as accurately as on correct trials, so the dimensionality collapse is not a failure to encode or remember the stimuli.
span.quote: Remarkably, the identity of the two visual cues could still be decoded with high accuracy in the error trials.

span.label: The error-trial collapse in dimensionality survives removal of the linear mixing component but disappears when the non-linear component is removed, so it is the non-linear mixed selectivity that weakens.
span.quote: The collapse in dimensionality that predicts the errors of the animal is specifically due to a weakening of the non-linear component of mixed selectivity.

span.label: The high dimensionality is not produced by grandmother-cell-like coding: the PFC representations are dense and the sparsest responses contribute little to it.
span.quote: We ruled out this scenario in our data by verifying that PFC representations are rather dense

span.label: Removing classical selectivity costs the most decoding accuracy early in the trial, and the loss shrinks as more cues are held in memory and the task becomes more complex.
span.quote: Note that removing classical selectivity causes a larger drop of decoding accuracy in the early epochs of the trial.

span.label: every task-relevant aspect can still be decoded after classical selectivity to it has been removed from every neuron
span.quote: Crucially, all task-relevant aspects can be decoded even when classical selectivity is removed.

span.label: the recovered accuracy grows as the task becomes more complex and more cues are held in memory
span.quote: As the trial progresses and more visual cues are memorized (i.e. the task becomes more complex), the accuracy progressively increases towards the values of the intact population.

span.label: the recorded representations reach the maximal dimensionality allowed by the design, d = 24
span.quote: For both epochs, N c grows with the size of the neural population N and it saturates near the value that corresponds to the maximal dimensionality.

span.label: simulated pure-selectivity populations fall orders of magnitude short of the recorded ones
span.quote: The asymptotic value of N c is always larger for the recorded representations than for the pure selectivity representations. The difference is several orders of magnitude for the two-object delay.

span.label: dimensionality collapses on error trials, as predicted before the test
span.quote: As predicted, the dimensionality decreases in the error trials.

span.label: cue identity is decoded just as well on error trials, so the collapse is not a failure to encode or remember the stimuli
span.quote: Remarkably, the identity of the two visual cues could still be decoded with high accuracy in the error trials. Fig. 5d shows that the cross-validation performances of the decoder of Fig. 3 trained on correct trials and tested on a hold-out set of correct (continuous line) and error trials (dashed lines) are indistinguishable, demonstrating that when the monkeys make a mistake, cue identities are encoded with the same strength as in the correct trials.

span.label: the collapse is due specifically to the non-linear component of mixed selectivity
span.quote: The collapse in dimensionality that predicts the errors of the animal is specifically due to a weakening of the non-linear component of mixed selectivity. Indeed, the difference in dimensionality between correct and error trials still remains significant after subtracting the linear component of mixed selectivity ( Fig. 5c ), whereas it is negligible when the non-linear mixed selectivity component is removed

span.label: the dense, non-sparse character of the representations rules out a grandmother-cell explanation
span.quote: We ruled out this scenario in our data by verifying that PFC representations are rather dense ( Supplementary Section S.11 ) and that the sparsest responses are not a major contributor to the observed high dimensionality

These neurons are said to have mixed selectivity to multiple task-relevant aspects of the task.
